title: The Armenian genocide (1915)
hookLine: Armenians, an old Christian people, are deported and killed under the Ottoman government; told carefully and honestly
last: SILENT NIGHT IN NO MAN'S LAND.

cards: A priest sits at a table with a notebook, writing down a song an old woman in a mountain village has just sung for him: a work song, sung while plowing.
He has been walking from village to village, saving tunes that were never written down. His name is Komitas, an Armenian priest and composer, and these songs are his people's memory.

Then one night, during the First World War, he is arrested in Constantinople along with other Armenian leaders, writers and clergy. Some of them never come back. Today is a hard day in the story, and I'll go slowly.

teach.b: The Armenians are an old Christian people, with their own church, their own alphabet and their own hymns, living in the lands of the Ottoman Empire.
During the First World War, the Ottoman government arrested Armenian leaders, then forced whole Armenian communities from their homes. Men were often killed near their towns.

Women, children and the old were marched toward the Syrian desert, and huge numbers died on the way, of killing, hunger, thirst and exhaustion. Assyrian and Greek Christians suffered in those years too.
Historians who study these years, the Armenian churches, and this lesson's title call it genocide: an attempt to destroy a people. The government of Turkey disputes that word.
Here it is told as survivors and historians have recorded it, with that dispute named, not hidden. Two more true things belong in the telling.
Survivors' accounts describe Turkish, Kurdish and Arab neighbors, Muslims, who hid Armenian families or took in orphans, sometimes at risk to themselves.
And Komitas survived the arrests, but the horror broke him, and he never composed again.
The songs he saved are still sung.

Matthew, telling of the children killed at Bethlehem, quotes the prophet Jeremiah: "Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." The Bible doesn't hurry past grief like that.
It lets it stand. The Armenian Apostolic Church has named the victims martyrs and saints, and Armenian communities gather each spring to remember them.
On a cross, a dying thief once asked for the same thing: "Lord, remember me." Remembering isn't revenge. It's refusing to let people disappear.

how: The Armenian Apostolic Church honors the victims as saints, and Armenian communities gather each spring for services, processions and the laying of flowers to remember them.

practice: Say the name quietly: Komitas, a priest who walked mountain villages saving songs, and lost his own voice to grief. Then let your mind widen to the families on the roads, whose names you don't know, and simply hold them.
If you pray, ask God to remember them; if you don't, let his name stand for all of them.
